---
title: "One model, fifteen dancers: vectorizing components"
---

![One spring-mass model, vectorized into a whole row of tuned oscillators](./assets/images/037/01_header.svg)

*I hope you've got your preferred drink in hand* ☕️🫖💧

You've seen the video. A row of pendulums — or in our case, springs and balls — released together. For a moment they move as one, then they drift apart into a travelling wave, split into little counter-marching packs, tie themselves in a knot, form (the illusion of) a double-helix… and then, as if nothing happened, snap back into a single line. 🌊

I wanted that in Modelica. Fifteen little spring-mass channels, each tuned to a slightly different frequency, dancing together. And here's the question that decides whether your afternoon is pleasant or miserable:

**are you going to build that model *fifteen times*?**

Please say no. Today we build it *once*, then let Modelica make fifteen copies for us — with fifteen different masses — in a single declaration. That trick is called **vectorizing components**, and once you have it, you'll reach for it constantly.

Let's dig in.

## Step 1 — build *one* thing, and build it well

Before you can have many, you need one. So we build a single channel: a spring, a mass, a guide rail to keep it moving vertically. Nothing fancy. Here's the skeleton of our [`Oscillator`](./assets/models/037/HarmonicMotion/Translational/Oscillator.mo) (I've trimmed the animation cosmetics):

```modelica
model Oscillator "A single vertical spring-mass channel"
  import Modelica.Mechanics.MultiBody;
  import Modelica.Constants.pi;

  parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Mass m = 0.5                    "Oscillating mass";
  parameter Modelica.Units.SI.TranslationalSpringConstant c = 10 "Spring stiffness";
  parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Length springLength = 0.5       "Rest height";
  parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Length amplitude = 0.15         "Initial lift";
  parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Position x = 0                  "Lateral position";

  final parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Time T_period = 2*pi*sqrt(m/c)
    "Natural period — 2π√(m/c)";

  MultiBody.Parts.Fixed        anchor(r = {x, 0, 0});
  MultiBody.Joints.Prismatic   prismatic(n = {0, -1, 0}, ...);
  MultiBody.Forces.Spring      spring(c = c, s_unstretched = springLength, ...);
  MultiBody.Parts.Body         ball(m = m, ...);
equation
  connect(anchor.frame_b, prismatic.frame_a);
  connect(prismatic.frame_b, ball.frame_a);
  connect(anchor.frame_b, spring.frame_a);
  connect(spring.frame_b, ball.frame_a);
end Oscillator;
```

Opened in System Modeler's **diagram** view, those four parts and their connections lay themselves out as one tidy channel — a fixed `anchor` up top, the `prismatic` guide, the coil `spring`, and the `ball` hanging at the bottom:

![The `Oscillator` component in System Modeler's diagram view — anchor, prismatic guide, spring and ball](./assets/images/037/05_oscillator_diagram.png){width=45%}

Two things I want you to notice, because they're what make the vectorization work later:

- **Everything that could differ from each variant is a `parameter`.** The mass `m`, the stiffness `c`, the lateral position `x`, the colours… all knobs on the outside. No magic numbers hiding in the equations.
- **There is no `inner World` inside.** `Oscillator` is a *component*, not a top-level experiment. It doesn't set up gravity or a coordinate origin — it just describes one channel and waits to be dropped into something bigger. (That's the same "component vs. system" distinction we drew back in [model refactoring](./005-ModelRefactoring.qmd). 😉)

Design your one thing so that *every difference is a parameter*, and future-you gets to be lazy. Which is the whole point.

> Hey, we never talked about what "inner" means! Well, we won't discuss it here — it's a topic for another day. For now, just know that `inner`/`outer` is how you share one object with many components.

## Step 2 — the copy-paste trap

Now the naïve instinct. You need fifteen of them, so… you type fifteen of them:

```modelica
Oscillator oscillator1(m = 0.47, x = 0.00, ballColor = {...});
Oscillator oscillator2(m = 0.49, x = 0.18, ballColor = {...});
Oscillator oscillator3(m = 0.51, x = 0.36, ballColor = {...});
// ... and so on, until your will to live runs out ...
Oscillator oscillator15(m = 1.01, x = 2.52, ballColor = {...});
```

It *works*. It's also fifteen places to make a typo, fifteen lines to touch when you want sixteen channels, and a `connect` statement graveyard to match. Want to change the stiffness for each spring? Fifteen edits. Want `n = 50` for a fancier wave? Enjoy. 🙃

When you find yourself numbering variables `foo1, foo2, foo3…`, something is wrong... and Modelica is quietly waving at you: *there's an array for that.*

## Step 3 — vectorize it

Here's the entire graveyard, replaced by one line:

```modelica
parameter Integer n = 15 "Number of oscillators";

Oscillator oscillator[n];
```

That `[n]` is the whole idea. `oscillator` is now an **array of components** — fifteen full `Oscillator` instances, each with its own spring, ball, joint and equations, all created from one declaration. Change `n`, and the count changes with it. One number. 🎉

And here's the lovely part — open the model's **diagram** in System Modeler and the whole array is a *single icon*. That one boxed component (top-right - yes I could have build a better icon... 😅) is all fifteen oscillators. It floats there unconnected because each channel is self-contained; the `world`, `rail` and `floor` on the left are the only shared scenery.

![The `MercuryWave` diagram in System Modeler — the single boxed component (top-right) *is* the array of fifteen oscillators](./assets/images/037/06_mercurywave_diagram.png)

You reach into the array exactly like you'd expect, with a one-based index:

```modelica
oscillator[1].prismatic.s     // position of the first channel
oscillator[15].ball.frame_a   // the connector of the last one
```

But an array of *identical* oscillators just gives you fifteen balls doing the exact same thing — a boring, synchronized bounce. The magic of the mercury wave is that each channel is *tuned differently*. So how do we hand fifteen different masses to fifteen instances in one go?

## Step 4 — `each`: the one keyword that makes it click

When you modify an array of components, every parameter you set has to answer one question: **"same for everyone, or one value per instance?"**

Modelica makes you say which, and the magic word is `each`:

```modelica
Oscillator oscillator[n](
    m                 = masses,        // ARRAY of n → one mass per channel
    springLength      = springLengths, // ARRAY of n → one length per channel
    x                 = x,             // ARRAY of n → one position per channel
    ballColor         = ballColors,    // ARRAY of n colours → one per channel
    each c            = c,             // SCALAR → broadcast: same stiffness for all
    each amplitude    = amplitude,     // SCALAR → same initial lift for all
    each ballDiameter = ballDiameter); // SCALAR → same size for all
```

Read that block slowly, because it's the heart of the whole technique:

- **`each c = c`** says *"give this one scalar value to every element."* The stiffness is shared, so we broadcast it. Without `each`, Modelica would expect `c` to be an array of `n` values and complain that a scalar doesn't fit.
- **`m = masses`** (no `each`) says *"here's an array of `n` values — hand element `i` to instance `i`."* Channel 1 gets `masses[1]`, channel 2 gets `masses[2]`, and so on.

So `each` = *"same for all"*, and a plain array = *"one apiece"*. 💡 That single distinction is what turns a boring row of clones into a tuned instrument. Get it wrong and the compiler tells you immediately — a scalar where it wanted an array, or vice versa — so it's a friendly mistake to make.

![`each` broadcasts one scalar to every instance; a plain array feeds one value per instance](./assets/images/037/02_scalar_vs_array.svg)

## Step 5 — where do the arrays come from?

As we mentioned before, `masses`, `x`, `springLengths`… these are arrays of `n` values, and you can either type them out by hand — it can be needed if the values are not following a pattern... - or instead we *compute* them, with an **array constructor** (a little `for` living inside braces):

```modelica
final parameter Real cycles[n] = {X + (n - i) for i in 1:n}
  "How many oscillations channel i does in the cycle time T";

final parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Mass masses[n] =
  {c*(T/(2*pi*cycles[i]))^2 for i in 1:n}
  "Mass of channel i, inverted from T_i = 2π√(mᵢ/c)";

final parameter Modelica.Units.SI.Position x[n] =
  {(i - 1)*dx for i in 1:n}
  "Lateral position: line them up dx apart";
```

Read `{expr for i in 1:n}` as *"build a list, letting `i` run from 1 to n."* It's the same comprehension idea you might know from Python. The physics — heavier balls swing slower, `T = 2π√(m/c)` — lives in *one* expression, evaluated `n` times. Change the tuning law in one place and all fifteen channels follow.

Even the colours come from a function that returns an `n × 3` matrix, so channel `i` gets its own hue:

```modelica
final parameter MultiBody.Types.Color ballColors[n] =
  HarmonicMotion.Utilities.rainbowColors(n);
```

And why do we see the *wave*. Here's an interesting 2D view, the eight of each fifteen balls at a few instants: at `t = 0` every ball is released together (flat blue line), and as the tuned frequencies drift apart the row folds into travelling-wave shapes. 🌊

![Vertical displacement across the row of balls at t = 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 s — a System Modeler simulation of `MercuryWave`](./assets/images/037/04_wave_snapshots.png)

> So each ball position over time is on a vertical line, and the same colour curves are the different balls at the same time.

## Step 6 — the tiny bit of plumbing

The last worry people have about vectorized components is *connections*. If you had to wire an array by hand you'd be back to fifteen `connect` lines — so Modelica lets you loop over them:

```modelica
equation
  for i in 1:n loop
    connect(something.port[i], oscillator[i].frame_a);
  end for;
```

In *our* mercury wave we actually didn't use this: each `Oscillator` carries its own `Fixed` anchor, so a channel is fully self-contained and needs no external wiring at all. That's not an accident — it's a direct payoff of the "build one thing well" rule from Step 1. The cleaner your component, the less plumbing the array needs.

## The END for today
Enough for today. We built one clean oscillator, stamped out fifteen of them with a single `[n]`, and used `each` to say what's shared and what's unique — no copy-paste, no numbered variables, one knob to rule the count. 😊


*Break is over, go back to what you were doing.*

Clem
